facts.text: Four families of sensor model are in use: physics-based signal-level models; simplified, statistical or phenomenological models; models learned from data; and hardware-in-the-loop stimulation.
facts.quote: Four families of sensor model are in use.

facts.text: The four sensor-model families form a continuum rather than competing alternatives; recent sensor-model validation literature and ASAM's project to define fidelity levels by sensor subcomponent use this kind of classification.
facts.quote: They form a continuum rather than competing alternatives, and the recent sensor-model validation literature and ASAM's project to define fidelity levels by sensor subcomponent both use this kind of classification [91].

facts.text: Physics-based, signal-level sensor models use ray tracing or ray launching for lidar, radar and ultrasonic sensors; physically based radiometric rendering for cameras and thermal cameras; full-wave or physical-optics solvers for radar; and acoustic ray tracing for ultrasonic sensors.
facts.quote: Ray tracing or ray launching for lidar, radar and ultrasonic; physically based (radiometric) rendering for cameras and thermal cameras; full-wave or physical-optics solvers for radar; acoustic ray tracing for ultrasonic.

facts.text: Physics-based, signal-level sensor models model material interaction, attenuation, multipath, optics and electronics.
facts.quote: Models material interaction, attenuation, multipath, optics and electronics.

facts.text: Physics-based, signal-level sensor models respond causally to changed geometry, materials, weather and sensor pose, allowing extrapolation to new machines and sensor positions.
facts.quote: Responds causally to changed geometry, materials, weather and sensor pose, so it can extrapolate to new machines and sensor positions.

facts.text: Physics-based, signal-level sensor models are interpretable.
facts.quote: Interpretable.

facts.text: Physics-based, signal-level sensor models have been validated for lidar rain and fog and for radar geometry.
facts.quote: Validated for lidar rain and fog and for radar geometry.

facts.text: Physics-based, signal-level sensor models need supplier internals and material data.
facts.quote: Needs supplier internals and material data.

facts.text: Error in physics-based, signal-level sensor models grows in heavy precipitation.
facts.quote: Error grows in heavy precipitation.

facts.text: Physics-based, signal-level sensor models are costly at high fidelity.
facts.quote: Costly at high fidelity.

facts.text: Dust and soiling are physically complex effects for physics-based, signal-level sensor models.
facts.quote: Dust and soiling are physically complex.

facts.text: Simplified physics in physics-based, signal-level sensor models can produce plausible but wrong output.
facts.quote: Simplified physics can still give plausible but wrong output.

facts.text: The recommended role of physics-based, signal-level sensor models in the collision-mitigation validation program is qualification-quality testing of important sensor effects and selected corner cases.
facts.quote: Qualification-quality tests of important sensor effects and selected corner cases.

facts.text: Simplified, statistical or phenomenological sensor models start from ideal geometry or detections and add range and angle noise, missed detections, false positives, dropout, analytical attenuation laws or image overlays.
facts.quote: Starts from ideal geometry or detections and adds range and angle noise, missed detections, false positives, dropout, analytical attenuation laws (Beer-Lambert, Marshall-Palmer rain distributions, ITU-R attenuation), or image overlays.

facts.text: Simplified, statistical or phenomenological sensor models can represent object lists with detection probability.
facts.quote: Object lists with detection probability.

facts.text: Simplified, statistical or phenomenological sensor models are very fast and easy to parameterize from measurements.
facts.quote: Very fast; easy to parameterize from measurements.

facts.text: Simplified, statistical or phenomenological sensor models are good for logic testing and scenario coverage.
facts.quote: Good for logic and scenario coverage.

facts.text: Simplified, statistical or phenomenological sensor models do not generate emergent effects such as radar ghosts, optical flare or realistic partial occlusion unless those effects are explicitly encoded.
facts.quote: Does not generate emergent effects such as radar ghosts, optical flare or realistic partial occlusion unless explicitly encoded.

facts.text: An ideal sensor model can look realistic at the tracking level yet show "the highest overall gap" at the raw-data level.
facts.quote: An ideal model can look realistic at the tracking level yet show "the highest overall gap" at raw-data level [36].

facts.text: Simplified, statistical or phenomenological sensor models are weak for edge cases.
facts.quote: Weak for edge cases.

facts.text: The recommended role of simplified, statistical or phenomenological sensor models in the collision-mitigation validation program is massive scenario sweeps and closed-loop function testing, once the model's validity domain is established.
facts.quote: Massive scenario sweeps and closed-loop function testing, once its validity domain is established.

facts.text: Sensor models learned from data use GANs, diffusion models, neural rendering such as NeRF and 3D Gaussian splatting, learned noise or measurement models, world models, or a learned real-to-synthetic transformation.
facts.quote: GANs, diffusion models, neural rendering (NeRF, 3D Gaussian splatting), learned noise or measurement models, world models, or a learned real-to-synthetic transformation.

facts.text: Sensor models learned from data can produce photorealistic output.
facts.quote: Photorealistic;

facts.text: Sensor models learned from data can re-simulate real logs.
facts.quote: re-simulates real logs;

facts.text: Sensor models learned from data reproduce complex distributions that are hard to hand-model.
facts.quote: reproduces complex distributions that are hard to hand-model.

facts.text: Sensor models learned from data are tied to their training domain and interpolate correlations without preserving physics.
facts.quote: Tied to the training domain; interpolates correlations without preserving physics.

facts.text: Harsh weather is often unsupported by sensor models learned from data.
facts.quote: Harsh weather often unsupported.

facts.text: Sensor models learned from data have weak extrapolation to new viewpoints.
facts.quote: Extrapolation to new viewpoints is weak.

facts.text: The validity domain of sensor models learned from data is hard to prove.
facts.quote: Hard to prove where it is valid.

facts.text: The recommended roles of sensor models learned from data in the collision-mitigation validation program are training data generation, replay editing, scenario variation, robustness testing, or a hybrid residual model around physics.
facts.quote: Training data, replay editing, scenario variation, robustness testing, or a hybrid residual model around physics.

facts.text: Hardware-in-the-loop sensor stimulation uses radar target simulators and scene emulators, lidar target emulators, camera video or raw-data injection or screen stimulation, and ultrasonic echo generators.
facts.quote: Radar target simulators and scene emulators, lidar target emulators, camera video or raw-data injection or screen stimulation, ultrasonic echo generators.

facts.text: In hardware-in-the-loop sensor stimulation, a real production sensor receives an artificial RF, optical, infrared or acoustic signal, or data are injected at a defined electrical interface.
facts.quote: A real production sensor receives an artificial RF, optical, infrared or acoustic signal, or data are injected at a defined electrical interface.

facts.text: Hardware-in-the-loop sensor stimulation exercises the real sensor, firmware, electronics and often the physical front end.
facts.quote: Exercises the real sensor, firmware, electronics and often the physical front end.

facts.text: Hardware-in-the-loop sensor stimulation is useful for proprietary black boxes.
facts.quote: Useful for proprietary black boxes.

facts.text: Hardware-in-the-loop sensor stimulation has limits on target count, distance, field of view and dynamics.
facts.quote: Limits on target count, distance, field of view and dynamics.

facts.text: Weather and soiling are mostly not reproducible through hardware-in-the-loop sensor stimulation.
facts.quote: Weather and soiling mostly not reproducible.

facts.text: Hardware-in-the-loop data injection after the sensor front end bypasses whatever lies upstream of the injection point.
facts.quote: Injection after the front end bypasses whatever lies upstream.

facts.text: Hardware-in-the-loop sensor stimulation is expensive and operates on one machine and sensor at a time.
facts.quote: Expensive; one machine and sensor at a time.

facts.text: The recommended role of hardware-in-the-loop sensor stimulation in the collision-mitigation validation program is final sensor and ECU regression testing, timing tests and supplier-independent characterization.
facts.quote: Final sensor and ECU regression, timing tests and supplier-independent characterization.
